about: Dated milestones of parent companies (buyouts, private equity owners, investigations, settlements, closures), each quoted from its sources. Read by inc/profile-timeline.php; each waits at Review inbox > Company milestones and shows on company and facility timelines only once approved. Researched 2026-10-14.

milestones.title: Bought Youth and Family Centered Services, a chain of programs for abused and neglected youth
milestones.detail: Acadia, then owned by Waud Capital Partners, acquired Youth and Family Centered Services, Inc. (YFCS) of Austin, Texas on April 1, 2011 from TA Associates. Fortune described YFCS as a provider of services for troubled children and adolescents with 13 facilities in nine states. Acadia's 10-K called it the largest private, for-profit provider of such services exclusively for abused and neglected children and adolescents.

sources.label: Acadia Healthcare Form 10-K for 2011, SEC
sources.quote: On April 1, 2011, we acquired Youth and Family Centered Services, Inc.

sources.label: Fortune, March 10, 2011
sources.quote: 13 facilities in nine states

milestones.note: Price not confirmed from a primary source (a deal database gives about $178 million).

milestones.title: Merged with PHC Inc. (Pioneer Behavioral Health) and went public on NASDAQ as ACHC
milestones.detail: Acadia completed its merger with PHC, Inc., which did business as Pioneer Behavioral Health, on November 1, 2011 and began trading on NASDAQ under the symbol ACHC. The combined company operated 34 facilities with about 1,950 licensed beds in 18 states.

sources.label: Acadia press release, SEC Form 8-K Exhibit 99.1, November 1, 2011
sources.quote: Begins Trading on NASDAQ under Symbol ACHC

milestones.title: Bought CRC Health Group, owner of the Aspen youth programs, from Bain Capital
milestones.detail: Acadia announced a definitive agreement to acquire CRC Health Group on October 29, 2014, describing CRC as the nation's largest specialized behavioral healthcare provider with 36 residential facilities and 84 comprehensive treatment facilities. The deal was valued at $1.175 billion in Acadia stock plus assumed debt; Bain Capital took Acadia shares. Acadia announced completion on February 11, 2015.

sources.label: Acadia SEC Form 8-K, October 29, 2014
sources.quote: On October 29, 2014, Acadia also announced the signing of a definitive agreement to acquire CRC Health Group, Inc.

sources.label: Acadia SEC Form 8-K, February 11, 2015
sources.quote: On February 11, 2015, Acadia also announced the completion of its acquisition of CRC Health Group, Inc.

sources.label: Treatment Magazine (ATIN), October 30, 2014
sources.quote: Bain Capital cannot be said to have exited the behavioral health space

milestones.note: Announced value $1.175 billion; Acadia's 2014 10-K (search result, not opened) gives total consideration of about $1.3 billion at closing.

milestones.title: Named in the Senate Finance Committee's 'Warehouses of Neglect' report on youth residential treatment
milestones.detail: The Senate Finance Committee's two-year investigation of youth residential treatment covered Acadia Healthcare along with Universal Health Services, Devereux Advanced Behavioral Health and Vivant Behavioral Healthcare. It reported rampant civil rights violations and heavy reliance on seclusion and chemical restraint.

sources.label: Oregon Public Broadcasting (Lauren Dake), June 12, 2024
sources.quote: rampant civil rights violations

milestones.note: Same report as the UHS entry.

milestones.title: New York Times investigation reports Acadia held psychiatric patients until their insurance ran out
milestones.detail: Jessica Silver-Greenberg and Katie Thomas of The New York Times reported, from more than 50 current and former executives and staff, that Acadia held patients against their will when it was not medically necessary, often until their insurance ran out. The article reported violations in at least 12 of the 19 states where Acadia ran psychiatric hospitals and described children assaulted or neglected at its Lakeview hospital in Georgia. Acadia denied improperly holding patients.

sources.label: The New York Times, republished by The Salt Lake Tribune, September 2, 2024
sources.quote: Unless the patients or their families hire lawyers, Acadia often holds them until their insurance runs out.

milestones.note: NYT original appears dated September 1, 2024 (Boston Globe reprint URL); the opened republication is dated September 2.

milestones.title: Received federal grand jury subpoenas and a prosecutors' request over admissions and billing
milestones.detail: On September 24, 2024 Acadia received a voluntary request for information from the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York and a grand jury subpoena from the Western District of Missouri; its subsidiary Lakeland Hospital Acquisition, LLC received another. The inquiries concern admissions, length of stay and billing practices, and Acadia said it expected similar requests from the SEC.

sources.label: Acadia SEC Form 8-K, September 27, 2024
sources.quote: related to its admissions, length of stay and billing practices

milestones.title: Paid $19.85 million to settle claims of billing for medically unnecessary behavioral health care
milestones.detail: Acadia agreed to pay $19.85 million to the United States and Florida, Georgia, Michigan and Nevada to resolve allegations that it billed Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE for medically unnecessary inpatient behavioral health services between 2014 and 2017 and failed to staff and supervise its facilities properly. The case began as a whistleblower suit by former employees. The claims were allegations only.

sources.label: Behavioral Health Business, September 26, 2024
sources.quote: knowingly billed for medically unnecessary behavioral health services and endangered patients

milestones.note: DOJ release (justice.gov/usao-mdfl) not fetchable by the tool.

milestones.title: Pine Tree Equity invested in Innercept
milestones.detail: Miami private equity firm Pine Tree Equity invested in Innercept, a Coeur d'Alene, Idaho residential treatment provider for adolescents and young adults, in February 2021. Pine Tree built Altior Healthcare from Paradigm Treatment Centers, Shortridge Academy, Innercept and Ironwood.

sources.label: PrivSource deal record
sources.quote: Miami-based private equity firm Pine Tree Equity invested in Innercept

sources.label: Behavioral Health Business, May 7, 2026
sources.quote: It has acquired Paradigm Treatment Centers, Shortridge Academy, Innercept and Ironwood.

milestones.note: Search summaries put Pine Tree's recapitalization of Paradigm in April 2019 (PrivSource), not opened. Dates for Shortridge and Ironwood not found.

milestones.title: Owner Pine Tree reported preparing a sale
milestones.detail: Axios reported, via Behavioral Health Business, that Pine Tree Equity Partners planned to auction Altior Healthcare, which ran Paradigm Treatment Centers, Patriot PowerUp and Ridge RTC with 500 employees in five states. Gladstone Capital had lent Altior $46 million in May 2025.

sources.label: Behavioral Health Business, May 7, 2026
sources.quote: lent Altior Healthcare $46 million in May 2025

milestones.title: Student Sergey Blashchishen, 16, died on his first day at SageWalk Wilderness School
milestones.detail: SageWalk, an Aspen program in Oregon, said a student died on August 28, 2009. Oregon's Department of Human Services opened an investigation and asked SageWalk to remove all students, and local police executed a search warrant. Salon later reported the boy, Sergey Blashchishen, died of heatstroke on his first hike.

sources.label: SageWalk statement, Strugglingteens.com, September 15, 2009
sources.quote: that occurred on August 28

sources.label: Salon (Art Levine), July 18, 2012
sources.quote: died of heatstroke on his very first school hike

milestones.note: Cause of death from Salon; an official autopsy ruling was not opened.

milestones.title: Oregon suspended Mount Bachelor Academy's license after confirming nine abuse and neglect allegations
milestones.detail: Oregon's Department of Human Services ordered Aspen's Mount Bachelor Academy to stop providing all services to children, after confirming nine child abuse and neglect allegations and more than a dozen rule violations. The state said the school posed a serious danger to children. Aspen was owned by CRC Health Group.

sources.label: The Bulletin (Bend), November 4, 2009
sources.quote: poses a serious danger to public health or safety of children

milestones.note: Search summaries say the school settled with the state in 2010 and the state withdrew its findings (not opened).

milestones.title: Closed five programs and consolidated three more
milestones.detail: Aspen announced it would close Bromley Brook School (VT), New Leaf Academy of Oregon, NorthStar Center (Bend, OR), Aspen Ranch (Loa, UT) and SunHawk Adolescent Recovery Center (St. George, UT). Aspen Achievement Academy was combined with Outback Therapeutic Expeditions, Youth Care moved to the Island View campus, and Passages to Recovery moved to Idaho. Aspen cited reduced demand in the economy.

sources.label: Aspen Education Group announcement, Strugglingteens.com, March 24, 2011
sources.quote: reduced demand for therapeutic schools and programs in today's economy

milestones.title: Bought CRC Health Group for about $742 million
milestones.detail: Funds managed by Bain Capital Partners completed the purchase of CRC Health Group on February 6, 2006, for total cash consideration of about $742.3 million including fees. Later that year CRC, with Bain's backing, bought Aspen Education Group.

sources.label: CRC Health Corporation Form 10-K for 2007, SEC
sources.quote: On February 6, 2006, investment funds managed by Bain Capital Partners, LLC

milestones.note: Same event as the CRC entry; listed here so Bain's timeline carries it.

milestones.title: Opened Rocky Mountain Academy in Idaho
milestones.detail: Rocky Mountain Academy, CEDU's first school in Boundary County, Idaho, opened in 1982. By 2004 CEDU's payroll put about $9 million a year into the local economy.

sources.label: Spokesman-Review, March 29, 2005
sources.quote: The opening of Rocky Mountain Academy in 1982 helped diversify Bonner County's timber- and agriculture-dependent economy

milestones.title: Sued over a student's treatment at Ascent and Northwest Academy
milestones.detail: A former student's family sued CEDU on June 27, 1996, in Monterey County Superior Court, alleging negligence, false imprisonment and fraud over his time at Ascent and Northwest Academy in Boundary County, Idaho, from December 1994 to May 1995. The suit said CEDU president Mel Wasserman misled the parents. CEDU did not comment.

sources.label: Spokesman-Review, July 11, 1996
sources.quote: The suit was filed June 27 in the Superior Court of Monterey County, Calif., headquarters of the CEDU Family of Services.

milestones.note: A lawsuit filing; outcome not found.

milestones.title: Paid $300,000 to settle claims over Northwest Academy
milestones.detail: CEDU paid a $300,000 settlement in 2002 to the families of two former students who alleged that Northwest Academy staff were poorly trained and abusive.

sources.label: Spokesman-Review, March 29, 2005
sources.quote: CEDU paid a $300,000 settlement in 2002 to the families of two former students who alleged that the staff at Northwest Academy was poorly trained and abusive

milestones.note: The Spokesman-Review attributes this to 'previous press accounts'.

milestones.title: Sued by more than two dozen parents
milestones.detail: In October 2004 more than two dozen parents sued Rocky Mountain and Boulder Creek academies, alleging misconduct and breach of contract.

sources.label: Spokesman-Review, March 29, 2005
sources.quote: More than two dozen parents filed lawsuits against Rocky Mountain and Boulder Creek academies in October, alleging misconduct and breach of contract.

milestones.note: Year inferred: the March 2005 article says 'in October'. Outcome not found.

milestones.title: Closed Rocky Mountain Academy
milestones.detail: Rocky Mountain Academy closed in February 2005, a month before the parent company's bankruptcy closed CEDU's remaining schools.

sources.label: Spokesman-Review, March 29, 2005
sources.quote: Even after the closure of Rocky Mountain Academy in February, the three remaining programs

milestones.title: Opened Kolob Canyon RTC, its second program
milestones.detail: Woodbury Reports said Bear River Residential Treatment Center in Utah was the first CERTS program and that a second, Kolob Canyon RTC, was scheduled to open March 1, 2002.

sources.label: Woodbury Reports, New Perspectives, February 2002
sources.quote: A second CERTS facility, Kolob Canyon RTC, is scheduled to open March 1, 2002.

milestones.note: Scheduled opening date; actual opening not confirmed.

milestones.title: Formed when Magellan sold its psychiatric hospitals to Crescent for $417.2 million
milestones.detail: Magellan Health Services, formerly Charter Medical Corporation, sold substantially all of its domestic acute-care psychiatric hospitals and residential treatment facilities to Crescent Real Estate Equities for $417.2 million in cash. At the same time Magellan and Crescent Operating formed Charter Behavioral Health Systems, LLC to run the hospitals, with Magellan holding 50%.

sources.label: Magellan Health Services Form 10-K for fiscal 1997, SEC
sources.quote: for $417.2 million in cash

milestones.note: The 10-K places the sale in the third quarter of fiscal 1997; a search summary of the same filing gives the closing as June 17, 1997, not seen in the text read.

milestones.title: 60 Minutes II hidden-camera report on Charter Pines Hospital
milestones.detail: CBS's 60 Minutes II sent a social worker with a hidden camera to work at Charter Pines Hospital in Charlotte, North Carolina. The report described doctors who barely spoke to patients, falsified records, dangerous conditions and no training in restraint. Charter then announced it would close two hospitals, and three Charter hospitals failed surprise state inspections.

sources.label: CBS News, 'Unsafe Haven', 1999
sources.quote: Falsified records. Dangerous conditions.

milestones.note: Page dated April 15, 1999; says first broadcast in March 1999. Page does not mention youth patients specifically.

milestones.title: Filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy after announcing the closure or sale of about 35 facilities
milestones.detail: Charter Behavioral Health Systems, then the nation's largest psychiatric hospital operator, filed for Chapter 11 in Delaware with less than $50 million in assets and more than $100 million in debts. A month earlier it had announced plans to close and sell about 35 facilities. Crescent Operating owned 90% of the company after Magellan's 1999 sale of its stake.

sources.label: California Healthline, February 17, 2000
sources.quote: the nation's largest psychiatric hospital operator

milestones.note: Its predecessor Charter Medical had a separate, brief Chapter 11 in 1992; not included.

milestones.title: Acquired by The GEO Group for about $62 million
milestones.detail: The GEO Group completed its acquisition of Correctional Services Corporation for approximately $62 million, or $6.00 per share. GEO kept CSC's adult facilities and sold the juvenile division, Youth Services International.

sources.label: GEO Group press release, November 7, 2005 (Form 8-K exhibit, SEC)
sources.quote: approximately $62 million, or $6.00 per common share

milestones.note: The release is dated November 7, 2005; GEO's later filings (search summary, not opened) give November 4, 2005 as the closing date.

milestones.title: Bought by Bain Capital funds for about $742 million
milestones.detail: Bain Capital agreed in October 2005 to buy CRC Health Group, then described as the biggest US provider of drug and alcohol treatment, for $720 million. Funds managed by Bain Capital Partners completed the purchase on February 6, 2006 for total cash consideration of about $742.3 million including fees.

sources.label: CRC Health Corporation Form 10-K for 2007, SEC
sources.quote: a total cash consideration of approximately $742.3 million

sources.label: UPI, October 13, 2005
sources.quote: will pay $720 million to buy California-based CRC Health Group

milestones.note: Headline price $720 million (2005 announcement); $742.3 million total including $28.5 million fees per the 10-K.

milestones.title: Bought Aspen Education Group, the largest for-profit chain of troubled-teen programs, for $279.5 million
milestones.detail: In November 2006 CRC acquired all of the stock of Aspen Education Group for about $279.5 million. CRC called it its largest acquisition to date. By the end of 2007 its youth division ran 29 programs in 10 states, including ten therapeutic boarding schools and ten outdoor programs.

sources.label: CRC Health Corporation Form 10-K for 2007, SEC
sources.quote: In November 2006, we acquired all of the outstanding capital stock of Aspen Education Group

sources.label: Salon (Art Levine), July 18, 2012
sources.quote: With Bain's backing, CRC purchased Aspen for nearly $300 million in the fall of 2006.

milestones.note: Deal announced October 2006 (VentureBeat, not opened); some sources put closing at end of September 2006.

milestones.title: Salon and The Investigative Fund report deaths and abuse at CRC and Aspen programs under Bain
milestones.detail: Art Levine's investigation reported deaths and state actions at CRC and Aspen programs, including the 2009 heat death of Sergey Blashchishen at SageWalk, Oregon's 2009 closure of two Aspen programs and the 2004 death of Matthew Meyer at Lone Star Expeditions. It said the Bain buyout left CRC with over $600 million in debt. CRC said the incidents were isolated, and Bain did not reply.

sources.label: Salon (Art Levine), July 18, 2012
sources.quote: In 2009, the state of Oregon forced the closing of two teen programs run by Aspen Education.

milestones.note: Reported with The Investigative Fund at The Nation Institute.

milestones.title: Closed three Eastern therapeutic boarding schools and two wilderness programs
milestones.detail: Aspen Education Group, part of CRC, announced it would close the Academy at Swift River (Cummington, MA), Talisman Academy (Hendersonville, NC), Stone Mountain School (Black Mountain, NC), SUWS Adolescent and Youth Programs (Shoshone, ID) and Adirondack Leadership Expeditions (Saranac Lake, NY) that summer. It cited families' inability to get credit or loans to pay for treatment.

sources.label: Aspen Education Group announcement, Strugglingteens.com (Woodbury Reports), July 10, 2013
sources.quote: the current market does not support us maintaining our entire network of therapeutic programs

milestones.title: Georgia jury awarded $50 million in punitive damages over a staff sexual assault
milestones.detail: A Cobb County State Court jury found Devereux liable for the 2012 sexual assault of a 15-year-old patient by an unsupervised employee at the Devereux Georgia Treatment Network in Kennesaw. Devereux said its staff uncovered the crime and reported it to police.

sources.label: Marietta Daily Journal, November 27, 2019
sources.quote: $50 million in punitive damages

sources.label: Marietta Daily Journal, November 27, 2019
sources.quote: was unsupervised when he assaulted the teenage female patient

milestones.note: Search summaries also cite $10 million in compensatory damages and a $55 million total; only the $50 million punitive figure was read on the page. Kind is a verdict, not a settlement.

milestones.title: Pennsylvania's governor ordered a state investigation of its campuses
milestones.detail: After the Inquirer report, Pennsylvania Gov. Tom Wolf directed the state Department of Human Services to investigate conditions at Devereux's Pennsylvania campuses.

sources.label: WHYY (AP), August 15, 2020
sources.quote: Pennsylvania Gov. Tom Wolf has directed the state Department of Human Services to investigate conditions at the firm's campuses in the state.

milestones.title: Philadelphia Inquirer found 41 children reported sexual assaults at its campuses
milestones.detail: A Philadelphia Inquirer investigation found that at least 41 intellectually disabled children had reported sexual assaults at Devereux campuses over 25 years. It reported that Devereux, with $467 million in annual revenue, understaffed its campuses and failed to supervise patients and staff. Devereux said it had added safeguards in the previous two years and later hired former U.S. Attorney General Loretta Lynch for a safety audit.

sources.label: The Daily Record (AP), August 12, 2020
sources.quote: at least 41 intellectually disabled children have reported sexual assaults over the past quarter-century

sources.label: City of Philadelphia, September 24, 2020
sources.quote: following a Philadelphia Inquirer report on August 11 about abuse at these facilities

milestones.note: No Washington Post investigation of Devereux was found; the 2020 investigation was the Inquirer's.

milestones.title: Philadelphia removed its 53 children from Devereux and closed intake
milestones.detail: Philadelphia's Department of Human Services and Community Behavioral Health announced they would remove the 53 Philadelphia children and youth in Devereux residential programs after increased monitoring, and immediately closed intake to new admissions. Devereux called the decision unjustified.

sources.label: City of Philadelphia, September 24, 2020
sources.quote: Currently 53 Philadelphia children and youth are in Devereux's residential programs.

sources.label: City of Philadelphia, September 24, 2020
sources.quote: DHS and CBH immediately closed intake to new admissions.

milestones.title: Founded by Jack and Ruth Eckerd with an outdoor therapeutic program for boys
milestones.detail: Jack and Ruth Eckerd founded the organization in 1968 and opened its first outdoor therapeutic (wilderness) program for boys in Florida. A girls' program, E-Nini-Hassee, followed in 1969, and the first juvenile justice program opened in 1982.

sources.label: Eckerd Connects, Our Legacy
sources.quote: Eckerd Connects was founded in 1968 by Jack and Ruth Eckerd.

sources.label: Eckerd Connects, Our Legacy
sources.quote: the organization opened its first juvenile justice program.

milestones.title: Became Eckerd Youth Alternatives, Inc.
milestones.detail: The organization took the name Eckerd Youth Alternatives, Inc. in 1998. It later operated as Eckerd Kids and then Eckerd Connects.

sources.label: Eckerd Connects, Our Legacy
sources.quote: Eckerd officially becomes Eckerd Youth Alternatives, Inc.

milestones.note: No dated source found for the later change to the Eckerd Connects name.

milestones.title: Merged with Caring for Children
milestones.detail: Eckerd merged with Caring for Children to form a nonprofit focused on foster care and other family services. It merged with Paxen in 2015 and ODLE Management in 2020, moving into workforce development and Job Corps.

sources.label: Eckerd Connects, Our Legacy
sources.quote: Eckerd and Caring for Children merge

milestones.title: Lost its Pinellas and Pasco child welfare contracts and gave up Hillsborough
milestones.detail: Florida chose not to renew Eckerd's child welfare and foster care contract for Pinellas and Pasco counties, and Eckerd said it would walk away from its $87 million Hillsborough contract in 2022. The Pinellas sheriff opened a criminal investigation after finding children housed in Eckerd's Largo offices in conditions he called as bad as those they were removed from; Eckerd admitted housing children in Hillsborough offices. More than 230 employees were told their jobs would end December 31, 2021.

sources.label: Tampa Bay Times, November 1, 2021
sources.quote: also will walk away from its $87 million Hillsborough contract in 2022.

sources.label: WUSF, November 10, 2021
sources.quote: The conditions are as bad or worse than the living conditions from which the children were removed.

milestones.note: Eckerd blamed inadequate state funding; the state cited failures (search summaries). This is foster care, not a TTI program, but it ended Eckerd's main Florida work.

milestones.title: Housatonic Partners invested
milestones.detail: Private equity firm Housatonic Partners first invested in Embark Behavioral Health in 2016 and reinvested in 2018.

sources.label: Behavioral Health Business, February 9, 2023
sources.quote: previously backed Embark Behavioral Health and first invested in the company in 2016

milestones.title: Consonance Capital Partners bought a majority stake
milestones.detail: Consonance Capital Partners acquired a majority stake in Embark Behavioral Health in a deal that closed in September 2022, valued by unnamed sources at about $400 million (12 to 15 times EBITDA). Embark then ran 27 programs at 40 locations in 15 states.

sources.label: Behavioral Health Business, February 9, 2023
sources.quote: valued at approximately $400 million

milestones.note: The February 2023 article says only 'The deal closed in September'; a later BHB article (January 2025) puts the acquisition at the end of 2022. Price not officially disclosed.

milestones.title: Cut about 60 jobs and closed sites in Los Angeles and Oregon
milestones.detail: In November 2024 Embark laid off about 60 people and closed several locations in Los Angeles and Oregon; three C-suite members left in January 2025. BHB reported that Embark had shut its wilderness program in 2023.

sources.label: Behavioral Health Business, January 24, 2025
sources.quote: It also closed several locations in Los Angeles and Oregon.

milestones.title: Bought by Galen Partners
milestones.detail: Healthcare growth equity firm Galen Partners acquired Evolve Treatment Centers, a Los Angeles-based adolescent behavioral health provider with 13 facilities in California, on January 8, 2020.

sources.label: PrivSource deal record
sources.quote: a Los Angeles-based provider of adolescent behavioral health services with 13 facilities across California

milestones.note: The GlobeNewswire press release (January 8, 2020) returned 403 and was not read. The company was then called Evolve Treatment Centers.

milestones.title: Founded
milestones.detail: Family Help & Wellness says it was founded to open a single wilderness therapy program and has served families since 2008.

sources.label: Family Help & Wellness, About Us
sources.quote: Since 2008, we've helped over 12,000 families.

milestones.note: Company's own site. Secondary profiles say it began in 2008 as Wilderness Training and Consulting LLC under Tim Dupell and Wayne Laird; not confirmed from a source I opened.

milestones.title: Trinity Hunt Partners invested
milestones.detail: Dallas private equity firm Trinity Hunt Partners made a growth equity investment in Family Help & Wellness in March 2014 on undisclosed terms. North Carolina Health News reported in 2025 that Trinity Hunt still held it after 10 years, twice as long as expected.

sources.label: PE Hub, March 31, 2014
sources.quote: Trinity Hunt Partners makes growth equity investment in Family Help & Wellness

milestones.note: PE Hub body is behind registration; the headline and date were read. Terms per North Carolina Health News (2025).

milestones.title: Closed WinGate Wilderness Therapy in Utah
milestones.detail: Family Help & Wellness closed WinGate Wilderness Therapy in Utah in August 2023 and Triple Divide Lodge in Montana in February 2024. A January 29, 2024 internal document described a nearly $7 million shortfall, ordered about $5 million in yearly cuts including 80 positions, and noted a debt payment due April 30, 2024.

sources.label: North Carolina Health News, June 14, 2025
sources.quote: Lender will not be in their happy place.

milestones.title: North Carolina moved to revoke Trails Carolina's license after a boy's death
milestones.detail: A 12-year-old boy died at Trails Carolina in Lake Toxaway, North Carolina, in early February 2024, less than a day after arriving; the death was ruled a homicide by asphyxiation and no charges were filed. On March 28, 2024, the state DHHS notified the camp it was revoking its license, citing five violations that endangered clients, and suspended admissions.

sources.label: WBTV, March 28, 2024
sources.quote: notified Trails Carolina on Thursday that its license was being revoked

sources.label: North Carolina Health News, June 14, 2025
sources.quote: Lender will not be in their happy place.

milestones.note: Search summaries say the final revocation letter was dated May 17, 2024, with an $18,000 fine (Carolina Public Press, not opened).

milestones.title: Asheville Academy closed after two girls died
milestones.detail: Two girls, ages 13 and 12, died by suicide at Asheville Academy in May 2025. The school shut May 31 and on June 4, 2025, voluntarily gave up its license and closed permanently.

sources.label: North Carolina Health News, June 14, 2025
sources.quote: voluntarily relinquished its license

milestones.title: Founded in Massachusetts as the state moved away from institutional care
milestones.detail: JRI was founded in 1973 in Massachusetts during the state's shift away from institutional care, and grew to more than 100 human services programs.

sources.label: Justice Resource Institute, About
sources.quote: JRI was founded in 1973 in response to massive, systemic problems.

milestones.title: Sued by former residents over sexual abuse at the Cresson Secure Treatment Unit
milestones.detail: Two former residents of the Cresson Secure Treatment Unit in Pennsylvania, which JRI ran for up to 52 juveniles from 2008 until Pennsylvania ended the contract and closed it in 2015, sued JRI for negligence over sexual abuse by staff. The suit quotes a 2010 U.S. Department of Justice report on the unit's rates of sexual victimization. The case was moved to federal court; a second suit followed in 2025.

sources.label: Altoona Mirror, October 26, 2024
sources.quote: some of the highest rates of sexual victimization reported by youth inmates

milestones.note: The 2025 second suit is from a search summary of an Altoona Mirror page (2025/02) that was not opened. No outcome found.

milestones.title: Bought Wake Forest University Baptist Behavioral Health
milestones.detail: Keystone, based in Nashville, completed its purchase of Wake Forest University Baptist Behavioral Health on January 11, 2005. Keystone then ran 24 nonresidential and 23 residential facilities in 10 states, serving about 3,000 young people daily.
programs: Wake Forest University Baptist Behavioral Health

sources.label: Wake Forest Baptist Medical Center news release, January 2005
sources.quote: has been concluded

milestones.title: Sold with its parent KEYS Group to Universal Health Services for $207 million
milestones.detail: UHS acquired KEYS Group Holdings, including Keystone Education and Youth Services, effective October 1, 2005, adding 21 residential treatment facilities, 21 therapeutic day schools and four detention facilities in ten states. The net price was $207 million in cash.

sources.label: UHS press release, October 10, 2005, via BioSpace
sources.quote: including Keystone Education and Youth Services, LLC

milestones.note: The prompt's idea that PSI bought Keystone is not supported; UHS was the buyer.

milestones.title: Opened KIDS of Bergen County in New Jersey
milestones.detail: Miller Newton, formerly Straight's national clinical director, opened KIDS of Bergen County in New Jersey in 1984 as the first KIDS program and the chain's headquarters; it later spread to El Paso, Southern California, Salt Lake City and Calgary.

sources.label: Breaking Code Silence, KIDS Centers of America (1984-1990)
sources.quote: This was first KIDS program to open, and was the headquarters of the organization.

milestones.note: Survivor-advocacy site; no primary source opened. Its headers give the chain 1984-1990 and Bergen County 1984-1998; it says KIDS of North Jersey closed in 1998 and New Jersey opened a Medicaid fraud investigation in 1999, both unconfirmed.

milestones.title: Two KIDS of Greater Salt Lake staff arrested after forcing a patient into a car
milestones.detail: Two peer counselors at KIDS of Greater Salt Lake were arrested in January 1990 for investigation of unlawful detention and assault after a 19-year-old patient who had left was allegedly forced into a car. The center suspended them pending an internal investigation.

sources.label: Deseret News, January 21, 1990
sources.quote: investigation of unlawful detention and assault

milestones.note: A Deseret News article of June 18, 1990, 'KIDS of Greater Salt Lake loses its license, will leave the area', is cited by Breaking Code Silence and Wikipedia but could not be opened.

milestones.title: Salt Lake program split off as Lifeline
milestones.detail: By August 1990 the former Salt Lake program operated as Lifeline Inc., which said it had separated from its parent organization, KIDS of Bergen County.

sources.label: Deseret News, August 21, 1990
sources.quote: But it has separated from Kids' parent organization, Kids of Bergen County (N.J.).

sources.label: Behavioral Health Business, July 20, 2021

sources.quote: which in 2017 backed Newport through its US Equity Opportunity Fund

milestones.title: Onex Partners bought about 60 percent
milestones.detail: Onex Partners V completed its purchase of about 60 percent of Newport Healthcare from the Carlyle Group in July 2021. Terms were not disclosed; PE Hub reported the value as $1.3 billion.

sources.label: Behavioral Health Business, July 20, 2021

sources.label: PE Hub, July 19, 2021
sources.quote: Onex completes Newport Healthcare buy at $1.3bn value
